title: The Dasam Granth question
hook: views differ on authorship of parts; devotion to Jaap and Chaupai is shared

segments.voice: Yesterday, the meat question: kutha forbidden by the code, and a langar where every plate can match. Your line was different plates. Did you leave someone's plate to them? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-four.

A gutka is a small prayer book, wrapped in cloth, kept on a high shelf. Open one that has been used for years and the paper tells on its owner. Certain pages are softer than the rest, gray at the corners from thumbs, morning and evening. In some gutkas, two of those worn places are Jaap Sahib and Chaupai. Neither comes from the Guru Granth Sahib. Both come from another book, the Dasam Granth, and that book carries one of the open questions of the panth.
screen: `A SMALL BOOK ON A HIGH SHELF.` → `TWO WORN PLACES.` → `A SECOND GRANTH, A SECOND QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Dasam Granth means the book of the Tenth, the tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh. It is a large collection: hymns of praise, long retellings of old stories, poetry about battle, and the Zafarnama, a letter to the emperor. Here the views differ. Some Sikhs hold that the whole collection is the Guru's own work. Others hold that parts of it, especially some of the long story sections, came from poets who gathered at his court. Others take a path between, accepting the prayers sung every day and studying the rest carefully. Scholars write books on it, and the conversation is sometimes heated. Now the part the sides share. Jaap Sahib is a cascade of short, rhythmic lines praising the Timeless One. It opens, here in paraphrase, by describing God as having no mark or sign, no color, no caste, no lineage. Chaupai is a prayer asking God's protection, plain and personal. The Sikh code of conduct places both among the daily prayers, the Nitnem: Jaap Sahib in the morning, Chaupai within the evening prayer. Both are recited when the amrit is prepared. So Sikhs who disagree sharply about the book's edges recite the same lines, morning and evening. That's a useful thing to notice about open questions. A question about authorship doesn't have to empty the prayer. People can keep studying a hard question and keep their thumbs on the same worn page.
screen: `DASAM GRANTH: THE BOOK OF THE TENTH.` · `VIEWS DIFFER ON WHO WROTE WHICH PARTS.` · `JAAP AND CHAUPAI: IN THE DAILY PRAYERS.` · `STUDY THE QUESTION, KEEP THE PRAYER.` · then, large: `NO MARK, NO COLOR, NO CASTE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold a question lightly. Settle, and breathe. Bring up one question you carry that doesn't have an answer yet. About faith, about family, about what's true. Instead of gripping it, set it in an open palm. Let your actual hand open on your knee if that helps. Breathe in, and let the question stay. Breathe out, and let it stop demanding a verdict today. If you pray, you can rest on the Timeless One, the one Jaap Sahib praises. The bell holds the time.
The Dasam Granth question. Sikhs differ on who wrote parts of the book of the Tenth, while devotion to Jaap Sahib and Chaupai is shared across the panth. Today's word.
Your line: shared devotion. Today, with someone you disagree with, find one thing you both still love, and say it out loud. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-four.
